Value
văl´ū
n. and v. (worth; to estimate the worth of; rendering Hebrew arak, Greek diaphero and timao)
Old French value, from Latin valere, to be strong, to be worth. In Leviticus it is the priest's estimate; in Matthew it is what a man is worth to God against sparrows, and what Christ was worth to the priests against silver.

Biblical Definition

“Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows” (Mat 10:31; Luk 12:7). Job to his comforters: “ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value” (Job 13:4). In the law of vows “the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, who art the priest, so shall it be” (Lev 27:12). And Matthew, on the thirty pieces: “they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value” (Mat 27:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines value as worth; that property of a thing which renders it useful or estimable; and, as a verb, to estimate the worth of; to rate.

expand to see more

VALUE, n. Worth; that property or those properties of a thing which render it useful or estimable; or the degree of that property or of such properties.

2. Price; the rate of worth set upon a commodity.

VALUE, v.t. To estimate the worth of; to rate at a certain price.

2. To esteem; to hold in respect and estimation.

Key Scripture

Mat 10:31 — "Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows."

Luk 12:7 — "But even the very hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not therefore: ye are of more value than many sparrows."

Mat 27:9 — "Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value;"

Job 13:4 — "But ye are forgers of lies, ye are all physicians of no value."

Lev 27:12 — "And the priest shall value it, whether it be good or bad: as thou valuest it, who art the priest, so shall it be."

Modern Corruption

Human worth is preached as a possession a man carries in himself, and Matthew 10 grounds it in a Father who counts sparrows.

expand to see more

The self-esteem gospel and Matthew 10:31 agree that a man is of great value and disagree about where the value lives. The modern doctrine locates it inside the man, as a dignity he owns and must learn to feel. The Lord locates it in the Father's attention: not one sparrow falls without Him, the hairs of your head are numbered, therefore fear not — you are worth more than many sparrows to the One who counts sparrows. Value in Scripture is conferred, not discovered; it is the price the Owner sets, and the verse was given to men about to be delivered up to councils and scourged, as the reason they need not fear. A dignity that comes from inside would not have helped them.

Matthew 27:9 records the valuation the other way. The chief priests, who knew the law of vows and the price of a slave, valued the Son of God at thirty pieces of silver — the sum Exodus 21:32 sets for a gored slave — and Zechariah had already called it “a goodly price that I was prised at of them” with the irony intact. Every man values Christ at something, and the price he sets is the truest statement of his own worth he will ever make.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew arak (H6186), to arrange, estimate, value; elil (H457), worthless, of no value; Greek diaphero (G1308), to differ, surpass in value; timao (G5091), to set a price on.

expand to see more

Hebrew arak (H6186) — to estimate, value; Leviticus 27:8, 27:12, 27:14.

Hebrew elil (H457) — worthless, nothing; Job 13:4, “physicians of no value.”

Greek diaphero (G1308) — to be of more value; Matthew 10:31, 12:12, Luke 12:7; timao (G5091), to value; Matthew 27:9.

Usage

"“Ye are of more value than many sparrows” — worth set by the One who counts sparrows."

"“The price of him that was valued” — thirty pieces, the price of a gored slave."

"“Physicians of no value” — Job's comforters."
